Q070.L1t: A quadratic function can model projectile motion, with a downward-opening parabola showing height changing over time.
Q070.L2t: The cannonball is above a given height exactly while the quadratic h(t) stays greater than that height, which is the interval between the two times it crosses that height.
Q070.L3t: Setting -4.9t^2 + 14t - 0.4 > 6 gives 4.9t^2 - 14t + 6.4 < 0, and the time above 6 meters is the gap between the two roots, which equals the square root of the discriminant divided by the leading coefficient, so sqrt(196 - 125.44)/4.9 = 8.4/4.9.
Q070.L4t: The cannonball stays above 6 meters for twelve sevenths of a second.
Q070.L2f: The cannonball's height follows a parabola that opens upward, so it dips to a minimum before rising again.
Q070.L3f: The time spent above 6 meters is the gap between the roots, and for this quadratic that gap works out to the discriminant 70.56 divided by 4.9 squared times 2, which comes to a little under one second.
Q070.L4f: The cannonball is above 6 meters for five sevenths of a second.

Q071.L1t: An equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three 60-degree angles, so its area can be found from the side length alone.
Q071.L2t: Dropping an altitude in an equilateral triangle splits it into two 30-60-90 right triangles, so the altitude is the side times the square root of 3 over 2.
Q071.L3t: The area is (sqrt(3)/4) times the side squared, so with a side of 12 it is (1.732/4) * 144, which is about 62.4.
Q071.L4t: The area is roughly sixty-two square inches.
Q071.L2f: The altitude of an equilateral triangle meets the base at a point one third of the way along it, splitting the triangle into two unequal right triangles.
Q071.L3f: The area of an equilateral triangle is about three quarters of the side squared, so for a side of 12 it is roughly 0.78 times 144.
Q071.L4f: The area is approximately 112 square inches.

Q072.L1t: Simplifying radical expressions with exponents relies on the laws of exponents, including rewriting roots as fractional powers.
Q072.L2t: A square root equals a power of one half, and multiplying powers of the same base adds their exponents while raising a power to a power multiplies them.
Q072.L3t: Since the square root of x^3 is x^(3/2), the product x * x^(3/2) is x^(5/2), and raising that to the fourth power multiplies the exponent by 4.
Q072.L4t: The simplified expression is x raised to the tenth power.
Q072.L2f: The square root of a power of x is found by doubling its exponent, so a radical always increases the exponent on x.
Q072.L3f: The lone x in front adds nothing to the exponent, and the radical of x^3 keeps its exponent of 3, so the base inside the parentheses is x^3 and only the fourth power remains to be applied.
Q072.L4f: The exponent of x in the simplified expression is twelve.
